Lecture A: myths and truths, anatomy of a neural network, a network from scratch

Lecture B: fully connected networks with Keras (MNIST)

Lecture C: convolutional neural networks, and beyond (RNN, embeddings, autoencoders)

::: notes - Adapted from the SCoRT short course (Deep Learning in R) and the previous 7-DLiR.FCN.CNN slides. Keras code is shown but not run when the slides are rendered (it needs TensorFlow); everything else is live R. - Course scripts: MNIST.R, MNIST-CNN.R, Image-Classification.R, Text-Classification.R, surres-mulogo.R. ::: # Lecture A: Neural Network Fundamentals {#part-a} ## Deep Learning: Myths and Truths :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - Often presented as algorithms that "work like the brain", that "think" or "understand". Reality is far from this. - **AI:** the effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans. - **ML:** rather than programmers crafting rules by hand, can a computer **learn the rules** by looking at data? - **DL:** ML with many successive **layers** of learned representations. ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![](images/dlir/AI-ML-DL.png){width="90%"} ::: :::: ## Classical Programming vs. Machine Learning :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/dlir/classical-programming.png){width="85%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/dlir/machine-learning.png){width="85%"} ::: :::: **Recipe of an ML algorithm:** input data points (sound files, images), examples of the expected output (transcripts, tags), and a way to **measure** the distance between current and expected output; this feedback signal adjusts the algorithm: **learning**. ## Anatomy of a Neural Network :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} - **Input data** and corresponding **targets** - **Layers**, combined into a network (model) - The **loss function**: the feedback signal used for learning - The **optimizer**: how learning proceeds (gradient descent via **backpropagation**) ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/dlir/nn-4.png){width="95%"} ::: :::: ## LeNet-5 and Why the 30-Year Gap :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - 1989, Bell Labs: Yann LeCun combines convolutional networks with backpropagation for handwritten digits; LeNet read ZIP codes for the USPS and checks (32x32 pixels) for banks. - 2011-2012: GPU-trained deep nets win ImageNet; AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Hinton) reaches 83.6% top-5 accuracy (vs 74.3% in 2011). - Three forces: **hardware**, **datasets and benchmarks**, **algorithmic advances** (ReLU, dropout, better initialization and optimizers). ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![](images/dlir/LeNet-5_architecture.png){width="100%"} ![](images/dlir/VGG16-2.png){width="80%"} ::: :::: ## A Neuron and Activation Functions A layer computes $\bz = \sigma(\bW\bx + \mathbf b)$: an affine map followed by an elementwise **activation** $\sigma$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} z <- seq(-4, 4, length = 400) acts <- cbind(sigmoid = 1 / (1 + exp(-z)), tanh = tanh(z), ReLU = pmax(z, 0), linear = z / 4) matplot(z, acts, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 3, col = c("#003366", "#C0392B", "#27AE60", "gray50"), ylab = expression(sigma(z)), main = "Activation functions") legend("topleft", colnames(acts), col = c("#003366", "#C0392B", "#27AE60", "gray50"), lwd = 3, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/21-dlir/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Linear Activation: Hidden Layers Disappear $$ \bz = \bW_1\bx + \mathbf b_1,\qquad \by = \bW_2\bz + \mathbf b_2 = (\bW_2\bW_1)\bx + (\bW_2\mathbf b_1 + \mathbf b_2). $$ A network with **linear** activations is just a **linear model**, no matter how many layers. Nonlinear activations are what make depth useful. ## Residual (Sur)Realism: The MU Logo Data An "inverse problem" dataset: $Y$ and five predictors constructed so that the **residual plot** of the linear model reveals a picture. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mu.logo <- read.csv("data/mu-logo.csv") dim(mu.logo) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10118 6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} lm.fit <- lm(Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5, data = mu.logo) plot(lm.fit$fitted.values, lm.fit$residuals, pch = ".", col = "#003366", xlab = expression(hat(Y)), ylab = expression(hat(e)), main = "Residuals vs fitted values") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/21-dlir/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Regression with a Neural Network A one-hidden-layer network with **linear** output (`nnet`, recommended package) should reproduce the linear fit: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(nnet) set.seed(4750) net0 <- nnet(Y ~ ., data = mu.logo, size = 0, skip = TRUE, linout = TRUE, trace = FALSE) # no hidden layer rbind(lm = coef(lm.fit), nnet = coef(net0)[c("b->o", paste0("i", 1:5, "->o"))]) |> round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) X1 X2 X3 X4 X5 lm 0.9761 0.1886 0.1204 0.9477 0.0123 0.967 nnet 0.9761 0.1886 0.1204 0.9477 0.0123 0.967 ``` ::: ::: - With `neuralnet::neuralnet(Y ~ ., hidden = c(10, 10), act.fct = function(x) x)`, the product of the weight matrices recovers the same coefficients (previous years' slides). ## A Two-Layer Network from Scratch: Backpropagation ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mlp_fit <- function(X, y, H = 10, lr = 0.05, epochs = 3000, seed = 4750) { set.seed(seed); p <- ncol(X); n <- nrow(X) W1 <- matrix(rnorm(p * H, sd = 1 / sqrt(p)), p, H); b1 <- rep(0, H) W2 <- rnorm(H, sd = 1 / sqrt(H)); b2 <- 0; loss <- numeric(epochs) for (e in 1:epochs) { A <- X %*% W1 + matrix(b1, n, H, byrow = TRUE); Z <- tanh(A) # forward pass yhat <- as.vector(Z %*% W2 + b2); r <- yhat - y loss[e] <- mean(r^2) g_yhat <- 2 * r / n # backward pass (chain rule) gW2 <- crossprod(Z, g_yhat); gb2 <- sum(g_yhat) gZ <- outer(g_yhat, W2); gA <- gZ * (1 - Z^2) gW1 <- crossprod(X, gA); gb1 <- colSums(gA) W1 <- W1 - lr * gW1; b1 <- b1 - lr * gb1; W2 <- W2 - lr * as.vector(gW2); b2 <- b2 - lr * gb2 } list(predict = function(Xn) as.vector(tanh(Xn %*% W1 + matrix(b1, nrow(Xn), H, byrow = TRUE)) %*% W2 + b2), loss = loss) } ``` ::: ## Fitting a Nonlinear Function ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); x <- sort(runif(200, -3, 3)); y <- sin(2 * x) + 0.3 * x + rnorm(200, sd = 0.2) fit <- mlp_fit(matrix(x), y, H = 15, lr = 0.1, epochs = 5000) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(fit$loss, type = "l", log = "y", lwd = 2, xlab = "epoch", ylab = "training MSE", main = "Gradient descent") plot(x, y, pch = 20, col = "gray50", main = "15 tanh hidden units") lines(x, fit$predict(matrix(x)), lwd = 3, col = "#C0392B"); lines(x, sin(2 * x) + 0.3 * x, lty = 2, lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/21-dlir/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: notes - This is exactly what Keras does, with automatic differentiation instead of hand-coded gradients, mini-batches (SGD), and better optimizers (RMSprop, Adam). ::: ## Some Neural Network Packages in R | Package | Description | |---|---| | `nnet` | feed-forward networks with a single hidden layer; multinomial log-linear models | | `neuralnet` | training by backpropagation; plots of the network | | `keras3` / `tensorflow` | interface to Keras 3 and TensorFlow (CPU/GPU/TPU) | | `torch` | native R interface to libtorch (no Python needed) | | `h2o`, `RSNNS`, `deepnet` | other toolkits | ::: tip `torch` for R installs without Python; `keras3` needs a Python environment (e.g. conda env `py39`) with TensorFlow. ::: # Lecture B: Fully Connected Networks with Keras {#part-b} ## Why TensorFlow and Keras in R? :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - **TensorFlow:** hardware independent (CPU, GPU, TPU), **automatic differentiation**, distributed execution, optimizers (SGD, Adam) that don't need all data in RAM, deployable models. - You define the graph in R; it is compiled, optimized, and executed; **tensors** flow between the nodes. - **Keras:** a user-friendly API; same code on CPU or GPU; quick prototyping. ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![](images/dlir/tensors_flowing.gif){width="80%"} ::: :::: ## Real-World Examples of Data Tensors | Tensor | Shape | Example | |---|---|---| | 2D | (samples, features) | tabular data | | 3D | (samples, timesteps, features) | time series, text | | 3D | (samples, height, width) | grayscale images (MNIST) | | 4D | (samples, height, width, channels) | color images | | 5D | (samples, frames, height, width, channels) | video | ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- array(runif(2 * 28 * 28), dim = c(2, 28, 28)) # a 3D tensor: two 28 x 28 "images" dim(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 28 28 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} flat <- matrix(aperm(x, c(1, 3, 2)), nrow = 2) # flatten each image row by row (like keras array_reshape) dim(flat) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 784 ``` ::: ::: ## Installing Keras ```{.r} install.packages("keras3") # or remotes::install_github("rstudio/keras3") library(keras3) keras3::install_keras(backend = "tensorflow") # needs Python (e.g. Anaconda / an existing conda env) tensorflow::tf_config() ``` - GPU support requires NVIDIA drivers, CUDA, and cuDNN: see . ## Developing a Deep Network with Keras: Four Steps ::: instructions 1. **Define the training data:** input tensors and target tensors. 2. **Define a network of layers** (a model) mapping inputs to targets. 3. **Configure learning:** a loss function, an optimizer, metrics to monitor (`compile()`). 4. **Iterate on the training data:** `fit()`. ::: ![](images/dlir/MNIST-2.gif){width="55%" fig-align="center"} ## Step 1: Data Preprocessing (MNIST) ```{.r} library(keras3) # MNIST: 60,000 training and 10,000 test images of handwritten digits, 28 x 28 pixels c(c(x_train, y_train), c(x_test, y_test)) %<-% dataset_mnist() # flatten images and rescale gray levels into [0, 1] x_train <- array_reshape(x_train, c(nrow(x_train), 784)) / 255 x_test <- array_reshape(x_test, c(nrow(x_test), 784)) / 255 # convert class vectors to binary class matrices (one-hot encoding) y_train <- to_categorical(y_train, 10) y_test <- to_categorical(y_test, 10) ``` ## Step 2: Model Definition :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ```{.r} model <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(784)) |> layer_dense(units = 256, activation = "relu") |> layer_dropout(rate = 0.4) |> layer_dense(units = 128, activation = "relu") |> layer_dropout(rate = 0.3) |> layer_dense(units = 10, activation = "softmax") summary(model) ``` ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![](images/dlir/dropout.gif){width="85%"} ::: :::: **Number of parameters:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} c(layer1 = (784 + 1) * 256, layer2 = (256 + 1) * 128, output = (128 + 1) * 10, total = (784 + 1) * 256 + (256 + 1) * 128 + (128 + 1) * 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` layer1 layer2 output total 200960 32896 1290 235146 ``` ::: ::: ## Softmax and Cross-Entropy $$ \text{softmax}(\bz)_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{10}e^{z_j}},\qquad \text{loss} = -\sum_{k=1}^{10}y_k\log\hat p_k\ \ (\texttt{categorical\_crossentropy}). $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} softmax <- function(z) { e <- exp(z - max(z)); e / sum(e) } # stable: subtract the max (Ch 13!) z <- c(2, 1, 0.1, 5, -1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0); p <- softmax(z); round(p, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.045 0.016 0.007 0.900 0.002 0.006 0.006 0.006 0.006 0.006 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} y <- c(0, 0, 0, 1, rep(0, 6)); -sum(y * log(p)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.1059 ``` ::: ::: - **Multi-class** (one label per image): softmax + categorical cross-entropy. **Multi-label** (several labels per image): sigmoid outputs + binary cross-entropy. ## Multi-Class vs. Multi-Label Classification ![](images/dlir/mcml-13.png){width="75%" fig-align="center"} ## Steps 3-4: Compile and Fit ```{.r} model |> compile( loss = "categorical_crossentropy", optimizer = optimizer_rmsprop(), metrics = c("accuracy") ) history <- model |> fit( x_train, y_train, batch_size = 128, # feed 128 samples at a time epochs = 10, # traverse the training data 10 times validation_split = 0.2 # hold out 20% for validation ) plot(history) ``` - `compile()` converts the layers to a TensorFlow graph, attaches the loss and optimizer, and arranges metric collection. ## Evaluation and Prediction :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ```{.r} model |> evaluate(x_test, y_test) model |> predict(x_test[1:100, ]) |> apply(1, which.max) - 1 # [1] 7 2 1 0 4 1 4 9 6 9 0 6 9 0 1 5 9 7 3 4 ... round(model |> predict(x_test[1:3, ]), 5) ``` Test accuracy is about 98% after 10 epochs. ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![](images/dlir/loss-acc.png){width="90%"} ::: :::: ## An FCN You Can Run Now: `nnet` on Handwritten Digits Same workflow (train/test split, softmax output, cross-entropy loss, weight decay = $\ell_2$ penalty) on a small simulated 4-class problem, with `nnet`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) centers <- matrix(c(0, 0, 3, 0, 0, 3, 3, 3), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE) lab <- sample(1:4, 800, replace = TRUE) X <- centers[lab, ] + matrix(rnorm(1600, sd = 1.1), ncol = 2) dat <- data.frame(x1 = X[, 1], x2 = X[, 2], class = factor(lab)) tr <- sample(800, 600) fit_nn <- nnet(class ~ ., data = dat[tr, ], size = 8, decay = 1e-3, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE) # softmax output mean(predict(fit_nn, dat[-tr, ], type = "class") == dat$class[-tr]) # test accuracy ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.835 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} g <- expand.grid(x1 = seq(-3, 6, length = 150), x2 = seq(-3, 6, length = 150)) g$pred <- predict(fit_nn, g, type = "class") ggplot() + geom_raster(aes(x1, x2, fill = pred), data = g, alpha = .35) + geom_point(aes(x1, x2, color = class), data = dat[-tr, ], size = 1.5) + coord_equal() + labs(title = "Decision regions of a one-hidden-layer softmax network") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/21-dlir/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## The Keras API: Layers - 90+ layers (and you can write your own): + **Dense:** `layer_dense(units = 64, kernel_regularizer = regularizer_l1(0.01))` (ridge/lasso penalties again!) + **Convolutional:** `layer_conv_2d()`, `layer_max_pooling_2d()` + **Recurrent:** `layer_simple_rnn()`, `layer_gru()`, `layer_lstm()` + **Embedding:** `layer_embedding()` + **Regularization:** `layer_dropout()`, `layer_batch_normalization()` ![](images/dlir/layers.png){width="45%" fig-align="center"} # Lecture C: Convolutional Neural Networks {#part-c} ## Why Not Fully Connected Networks for Images? 1. **Too many weights:** a $100\times140\times3$ color image has 42,000 inputs; 100 hidden nodes need 4,200,000 weights in the first layer alone $\Rightarrow$ more data needed, overfitting, slow training. 2. **Flattening destroys spatial structure:** neighboring pixels are correlated in 2-D. **Convolution** uses small filters shared across the image: few parameters, **local** and **translation-invariant** features. ## Convolution in 1-D In deep learning "convolution" is really **cross-correlation** (no flip): $(x * w)_i = \sum_k x_{i+k}w_k$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} conv1d <- function(x, w) sapply(1:(length(x) - length(w) + 1), function(i) sum(x[i:(i + length(w) - 1)] * w)) x <- c(0, 1, 2, 3, 3); w <- c(2, -1, 1) conv1d(x, w) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 3 4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} convolve(x, w, type = "filter") # base R agrees ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 3 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: notes - The old slides illustrated the mathematical convolution (with the flip). Keras layers compute cross-correlation; since the filters are learned, the distinction does not matter. ::: ## Convolution in 2-D: Feature Maps ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} conv2d <- function(img, k, stride = 1, pad = 0) { if (pad > 0) { img2 <- matrix(0, nrow(img) + 2 * pad, ncol(img) + 2 * pad) img2[(pad + 1):(pad + nrow(img)), (pad + 1):(pad + ncol(img))] <- img; img <- img2 } f <- nrow(k); out_r <- (nrow(img) - f) %/% stride + 1; out_c <- (ncol(img) - f) %/% stride + 1 out <- matrix(0, out_r, out_c) for (i in 1:out_r) for (j in 1:out_c) { r <- (i - 1) * stride + 1; c <- (j - 1) * stride + 1 out[i, j] <- sum(img[r:(r + f - 1), c:(c + f - 1)] * k) } out } img <- volcano[seq(1, 87, 2), seq(1, 61, 2)] / max(volcano) sobel_x <- matrix(c(-1, 0, 1, -2, 0, 2, -1, 0, 1), 3, byrow = TRUE) fm <- conv2d(img, sobel_x); relu <- pmax(fm, 0) par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1)) image(img, axes = FALSE, main = "input", col = gray.colors(50)); image(fm, axes = FALSE, main = "conv (Sobel x)", col = hcl.colors(50)) image(relu, axes = FALSE, main = "ReLU(conv)", col = hcl.colors(50)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/21-dlir/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Stride, Padding, and Output Size $$ \text{Output size} = \frac{N - F + 2P}{S} + 1 $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} outsize <- function(N, F, S, P = 0) (N - F + 2 * P) / S + 1 rbind(stride1 = outsize(7, 3, 1), stride2 = outsize(7, 3, 2), stride3 = outsize(7, 3, 3), # 5, 3, 2.33 (invalid!) pad1 = outsize(7, 3, 1, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] stride1 5.000 stride2 3.000 stride3 2.333 pad1 7.000 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} dim(conv2d(matrix(1:49, 7), matrix(1, 3, 3), stride = 2)); dim(conv2d(matrix(1:49, 7), matrix(1, 3, 3), pad = 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 3 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 7 7 ``` ::: ::: - Without padding the volume shrinks quickly ($32\to28\to24$ with $5\times5$ filters); **zero padding** keeps the size. - Common settings: $F = 3, S = 1, P = 1$; $F = 5, S = 1, P = 2$; number of filters $K = 32, 64, 128$. ## Max Pooling Downsample each feature map: $2\times2$ windows, stride 2, keep the maximum ($100\times100\times128\to50\times50\times128$). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} maxpool <- function(m, f = 2, s = 2) { r <- (nrow(m) - f) %/% s + 1; c <- (ncol(m) - f) %/% s + 1 outer(1:r, 1:c, Vectorize(function(i, j) max(m[((i - 1) * s + 1):((i - 1) * s + f), ((j - 1) * s + 1):((j - 1) * s + f)]))) } m <- matrix(c(1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 3, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4), 4, byrow = TRUE) m; maxpool(m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [1,] 1 1 2 4 [2,] 5 6 7 8 [3,] 3 2 1 0 [4,] 1 2 3 4 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [1,] 6 8 [2,] 3 4 ``` ::: ::: ## CNN Architecture: Review ![](images/dlir/cnn-2.gif){width="40%" fig-align="center"} - **Input:** raw pixels, e.g. $32\times32\times3$. - **Conv layer:** $K$ filters $\Rightarrow$ $32\times32\times K$ feature maps (learned features, no hand-designed features). - **ReLU:** elementwise $\max(0,x)$; size unchanged. - **Pooling:** spatial downsampling, e.g. $16\times16\times K$. - **Fully connected + softmax:** class probabilities (e.g. doors 0.1, stairs 0.1, signs 0.8). ## A CNN for MNIST in Keras ```{.r} x_train <- array_reshape(x_train, c(nrow(x_train), 28, 28, 1)) / 255 # keep the 2-D structure! cnn <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(28, 28, 1)) |> layer_conv_2d(filters = 32, kernel_size = c(3, 3), activation = "relu") |> layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = c(2, 2)) |> layer_conv_2d(filters = 64, kernel_size = c(3, 3), activation = "relu") |> layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = c(2, 2)) |> layer_flatten() |> layer_dropout(rate = 0.5) |> layer_dense(units = 10, activation = "softmax") cnn |> compile(loss = "categorical_crossentropy", optimizer = "adam", metrics = "accuracy") cnn |> fit(x_train, y_train, batch_size = 128, epochs = 15, validation_split = 0.1) ``` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # parameters: conv1 (3*3*1+1)*32, conv2 (3*3*32+1)*64, dense (5*5*64+1)*10 c(conv1 = (3 * 3 * 1 + 1) * 32, conv2 = (3 * 3 * 32 + 1) * 64, dense = (5 * 5 * 64 + 1) * 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` conv1 conv2 dense 320 18496 16010 ``` ::: ::: Far fewer parameters than the 235,146 of the FCN, and about 99% test accuracy. Demo: . ## Beyond CNNs: Recurrent Networks and Embeddings :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ```{.r} rnn <- keras_model_sequential() |> layer_lstm(units = 128, input_shape = c(timesteps, features)) |> layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "sigmoid") txt <- keras_model_sequential() |> layer_embedding(input_dim = 10000, output_dim = 8) |> layer_flatten() |> layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "sigmoid") ``` - **RNN/LSTM:** sequences, long-term dependencies (sentiment, forecasting) - **Embeddings:** dense word vectors learned jointly with the task, or pre-trained (word2vec, GloVe) ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![](images/dlir/embedding.png){width="95%"} ::: :::: ## Autoencoders: Nonlinear PCA :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ```{.r} ae <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(784)) |> layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |> layer_dense(units = 32, activation = "relu") |> # bottleneck layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |> layer_dense(units = 784, activation = "sigmoid") ae |> compile(loss = "mse", optimizer = "adam") ae |> fit(x_train, x_train, epochs = 20) # input = target ``` - With **linear** activations and MSE loss, an autoencoder spans the same subspace as **PCA** (deck 08)! - Applications: dimension reduction, denoising, anomaly detection, inpainting; functional autoencoders for curves. ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![](images/dlir/autoencoder.gif){width="95%"} ::: :::: ## Advanced Topics and Deployment - **Transfer learning:** `application_resnet50()`, fine-tuning pre-trained networks - Custom layers and callbacks (early stopping: `callback_early_stopping()`) - Generative models: variational autoencoders, GANs, text generation - Saving and loading: `save_model(model, "model.keras")`, `load_model()` - Deployment: Plumber APIs, TensorFlow Serving, **Shiny** (deck 10) ## Python Supplement: The Same FCN in Keras (Python) ```{.python} import keras (x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = keras.datasets.mnist.load_data() x_train = x_train.reshape(-1, 784) / 255 model = keras.Sequential([ keras.Input(shape=(784,)), keras.layers.Dense(256, activation="relu"), keras.layers.Dropout(0.4), keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"), keras.layers.Dropout(0.3), keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")]) model.compile(loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", optimizer="rmsprop", metrics=["accuracy"]) model.fit(x_train, y_train, batch_size=128, epochs=10, validation_split=0.2) ``` The R `keras3` code is a thin layer over exactly this Python library. ## Summary and Readings ::: instructions - A network = layers (affine map + nonlinear activation) + loss + optimizer; trained by backpropagation + (stochastic) gradient descent. - Linear activations collapse to a linear model; depth needs nonlinearity. - Keras workflow: data tensors $\rightarrow$ `keras_model_sequential()` $\rightarrow$ `compile()` $\rightarrow$ `fit()` $\rightarrow$ `evaluate()`/`predict()`. - CNNs: shared local filters, stride, padding, pooling; far fewer parameters than FCNs for images. ::: - F. Chollet, T. Kalinowski, J. J. Allaire, *Deep Learning with R*, 2nd ed., Manning. - Keras for R: ; cheatsheet: - Stanford CS231n notes:

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
